cells.C: Welcome to Week 1 and your Literature Review Course! This week's discussion will not be difficult but is critical for a few reasons: (1) it will assist your instructor with knowing where you are in the course of your researching the literature; (2) it will help you reflect on where you are and how you might progress this term; and (3) it will establish a presence for you in the courseroom to ensure that you are not dropped from the course. To meet the requirements of this discussion, please post the following:

Write a brief note about where you are in your journey toward your dissertation. This can be one paragraph, and discuss any barriers, hurdles, or concerns you have about the next steps of your process.
Explain the topic that you are exploring, analyzing, and researching (in no more than five sentences). Cite at least two sources to help explain/support your topic.
Attach a list of the sources you have already compiled for your project.
Feel free to respond to your classmates' posts (not required).

It’s great to see so many of you from previous courses. I appreciate how our courses add to our previous research. I am refining my research question and integrating my problem statement, conceptual framework, and methodological approach. I feel confident in my study’s direction; a primary challenge involves ensuring my framing remains qualitative and focuses on perceptions rather than causality. This requires constant care in language and design. I am also narrowing my literature to recent, U.S.-based empirical studies, while continuing depth and rigor. Moving forward, I am strengthening coherence between the Leader–Member Exchange (LMX) theory and managers’ lived experiences in remote environments while I prepare for data collection. The process feels iterative and purposeful, and I gain more clarity with each revision.

My research explores how managers in U.S.-based technology companies perceive and enact inclusive leadership in completely remote sociotechnical work systems. The study uses Leader–Member Exchange (LMX) theory to understand how leader-member relationships shape inclusion, access, and engagement in remote contexts. Recent studies suggest remote work creates disparities in communication, visibility, and support. This makes leadership behaviors more critical to the employee experience (Chen, 2024; Nyberg, 2021). Other research shows that leader support and relationship interactions impact worker well-being and job satisfaction in distributed environments (Becker et al., 2022). By focusing on managerial perceptions, this study intends to understand how inclusive leadership is interpreted and practiced in digitally mediated workplaces.

At this stage of my dissertation journey, I have developed a much clearer direction, while working through some key finer details. I have refined my topic, problem and research question and I feel better overall. However, one of my major difficulties is ensuring that my study remains focused on perceptions (rather than moving into experiences or objective results), which are very easy to do in this area. I continue to refine my theoretical framework and my research design in a manner that makes both feasible. Additionally, I am working on narrowing my target population and formulating how best to reach those participants. Overall, I feel as if I am in good shape, but I know that maintaining precision and alignment will be critical to my progress moving forward.

This study is investigating how accounting professionals perceive organizations’ practices that relate to fraud risk and the effectiveness of internal controls. Previous studies have established a link between internal control weaknesses and increased risk to the overall organization as well as how an auditor will respond to those risks, therefore it is important to understand the way these practices are viewed in actual field settings (Elder et al., 2009). Previous studies have also shown that ethical infrastructure (i.e., training, reporting systems, organizational policies) has a substantial influence on accountants’ ethical judgment and decision-making processes (Seifert et al., 2022). Further, accountants’ decisions regarding fraudulent financial statements will be influenced by their attitudes toward risk-taking, social pressures, and perceived control, providing further impetus for the need to study practitioners’ perceptions (Carpenter & Reimers, 2005). This study will provide a better understanding of how accounting professionals interpret and apply these organizational practices in real-world settings.

My dissertation is in the early stages of construction.  Having just completed RSCH 8926, my project plan is just beginning to take shape.  Desiring to expand on a proposed study of Stakeholder-Salience Governance of ITDRPaaS in SMEs: via Aligning IT Strategy and Decision Rights Governance. My knowledge of specific research is just coming into focus, as my improving alignment toward research/understanding of how IT Network managers effectively make decisions under stakeholder-salience conditions, power, legitimacy, and urgency dynamically shape who is authorized to decide, how escalation unfolds, and what constitutes acceptable proof of recover-ability when urgency intensifies (Freeman et al., 2020; Lowry et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 1997).

My research focuses on stakeholder salience theory operationalized prioritization through attributes of power, legitimacy, and urgency (Freeman. 1984; Mitchell et al., 1997), understanding how from a continued review of literature explains why some stakeholder demands for immediate recover ability to system capability are treated as non-negotiable while others are deferred or underfunded (Mitchell et al., 1997).  Specific to addressing challenges, organizations  have with utilizing technological tools without the tied phenomenology (Creswell & Poth, 2018), adaptive management strategies, and organizational policies to support distributed development teams. Aligning to restated 30 year theory of Peter Senge’s theory of learning how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) either lack a formally established disaster recovery plan or fail to embed recovery capabilities within enforceable governance structures (Örtenblad, 2007), resulting in inconsistent and difficult-to-demonstrate recoverability during connection disruption(s).

Last semester, I completed RSCH8926, where I laid out my project plan. At this stage, while I have a good idea of the direction my dissertation should take in terms of literature and methodology, I do need to expand both the theoretical and empirical frameworks. Cabinova et al. (2024) demonstrated that many of the top-ranked nations in global innovation rankings are misusing and underutilizing resources entering their national innovation systems. These findings cannot be generalized across national income categories; therefore, the proposed study will test the hypothesis of resource underutilization using the World Bank data and structures within emerging economies. A major hurdle is aligning datasets across a wide category of emerging countries.

The proposed study examines innovation efficiency, a subset of the well-established concept of total factor productivity (TFP) in the efficiency modelling literature (Perelman, 1995). TFP is an implicit efficiency measure for determining the input-output productivity within the supply chains of productive sectors (Chen and Shao, 2025). The study will assess the utilization of resources entering the national innovation systems based on the innovation value chain theory (Cao et al., 2025). The study will employ a quantitative regression analysis to examine innovation efficiency in the supply chains of emerging markets (e.g., Brazil, India, China, Indonesia, Nigeria, and South Africa) using Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) regression models (Zhou et al., 2024). This will attempt to establish the relationships among government, innovation efficiency, innovation total factor productivity, and decomposition terms (technical efficiency, efficiency index change, returns to scale, and projection terms).

At this point in my doctoral journey, I have developed the focus for my research and begun building a strong foundation of scholarly sources for my dissertation. My main focus is now refining my literature search and organizing sources for my literature review. One challenge I anticipate is ensuring that my literature review is both comprehensive and criticality synthesized rather than descriptive. Additionally, balancing the depth of research with time management will be important as I continue progressing.

My proposed study explores how human resource leaders and supervisors describe and interpret their efforts to foster a sense of belonging among remote millennial workers in the U.S. healthcare industry. This topic is significant as organizations continue to adapt to remote work while addressing employee engagement and inclusion. Research shows that a sense of belonging is closely related to employee engagement, job satisfaction, and retention outcomes (Guest, 2017). Additionally, leadership practices play an important role in shaping inclusive work environments and influencing employee perceptions of support and connection (Yang et al., 2020). This study aims to contribute to the literature by examining leadership strategies that promote belonging in remote healthcare settings.

Like most of my classmates, I’m in the beginning phase of my dissertation. So far, I have identified a topic and problem and have an approved project plan. In addition, I have read and collected numerous articles relevant to my topic. The difficulty in searching for articles relevant to the topic is the proliferation of AI articles that focus on the application of AI rather than on the system development processes used to create AI. The future challenge is how to organize and synthesize the articles to tell the story of my topic and its pertinent themes, guiding the reader into the study.

The topic of study is the software development methodologies and processes used for developing large AI applications or systems. Currently, the majority of technology organizations’ AI development projects are deemed failures because they never become production-ready (Hamer et al., 2021; Vial et al., 2021). Researchers such as Vial et al. (2021) assert that the issue is related to data-handling processes, whereas Hamer et al. (2021) assert that the failure rate is due to project management processes. The purpose of the study is to explore the processes currently used in developing complex AI systems.
Hamer, P., Idoine, C., Vashisth, S., Choudhary, F., Jaffri, A., & Krensky, P. (2021). The State of Data Science and Machine Learning. Gartner Inc.,
Vial, G., Jiang, J., Giannelia, T., & Cameron, A. (2021). The Data Problem Stalling AI. MIT Sloan Management Review, 62(2), 47–53.

I am currently in the early stages of my dissertation journey where I have developed my topic, problem statement, and started building my literature review. Right now I am focused on refining my research direction and continuing to gather and organize sources. One challenge I am facing is making sure my study clearly addresses a meaningful research gap while still staying aligned with my qualitative approach. I also want to improve how I synthesize my sources instead of just summarizing them. Moving forward, my goal is to strengthen my literature review and feel more confident in my research design.

My research focuses on how project managers perceive and use behavioral practices while managing execution demands during the implementation of operational initiatives. I am looking at how they coordinate stakeholders, handle interdependent tasks, and respond to changing project conditions. Research shows that managerial behaviors influence coordination and overall project outcomes (Tawse et al., 2024). However, much of the existing research focuses on quantitative relationships rather than how project managers actually experience these situations. Prior studies also highlight the importance of leadership effectiveness in project success (Zwikael & Meredith, 2021). My study aims to explore those lived experiences and perspectives in more depth.

Tawse, A., Atwater, L., Vera, D., & Werner, S. (2024). Strategy implementation: The role of middle manager leadership and coordination. Journal of Strategy and Management, 17(1), 59–77. https://doi.org/10.1108/JSMA-01-2023-0007Links to an external site.

My dissertation investigates how IT decision-makers in large U.S. corporations integrate generative AI (GenAI) to enhance employee performance and development. The research identifies organizational strategies and perspectives to determine if GenAI is a viable tool for workforce advancement. By evaluating these adoptions, the study assesses the potential of GenAI to bolster overall organizational outcomes. My primary concern regarding the upcoming dissertation phases is participant recruitment, as engaging high-level professionals may be difficult. I am currently refining my questionnaire for formal review and plan to utilize NVivo for data analysis. Although my technical proficiency with the software is currently at an introductory level after a recent course, I anticipate gaining sufficient practical experience before the analysis stage.

The central phenomenon is the process of incorporating generative AI solutions as a knowledge management enhancement to support employee development and performance. The general problem is that large US corporations struggle to integrate GenAI into their core operations, hindering their ability to leverage its potential to improve employee performance, access to knowledge, and scalable development programs (Appio et al., 2024; McClure, 2024). Employing a qualitative inductive thematic analysis, this research will highlight GenAI's technical power, economic potential, and organizational risks. Kanback et al. (2024) assert that GenAI is a vital catalyst for market leadership, requiring businesses to adapt their internal models and navigate technical integration strategies, systemic effects, and trust-related risks as identified by IT decision-makers. Story (2025) emphasizes that while GenAI revolutionizes efficiency, its success depends on understanding its dual influence on knowledge management systems and individual workers.
Appio, F. P., Frattini, F., & Urbinati, A. (2024). AI in business operations: driving urban growth and societal sustainability. BMC Research Notes, 17(1), 216.

Kanbach, D. K., Heiduk, L., Blueher, G., Schreiter, M., & Lahmann, A. (2024). The GenAI is out of the bottle: generative artificial intelligence from a business model innovation perspective. For my dissertation, the research topic and study were approved by the endorser. It was a great relief to hear that my study was approved and a positive reinforcement for my work. My concern is how to integrate the Work Day Questionnaire (WDQ) as a key construct into Qualtrics for the survey. The endorser has approved my use of the WDQ, a 77-question survey that, when completed, offers insights into workers' levels of job autonomy. However, some of the questions do not seem to fit the study. I chose Qualtrics because it allows users to use a five-point Likert scale and a matrix table question type, which aligns with the WDQ. I need some guidance and help with setting up the survey in Qualtrics. WDQ In Qualtrics.Download WDQ In Qualtrics.

The topic of my dissertation is a quantitative investigation of knowledge management (KM) and its impact on training among early-career professionals, with potential implications for accounting departments. The problem to be explored is higher direct costs attributable to accounting inaccuracies (KPMG, 2023), noncompliance (GAO, 2025), inconsistencies (Ayodele et al., 2023), and information asymmetry (Arkhipova et al., 2024), as illustrated in Figure 1. The specific problems are accounting inaccuracies (KPMG, 2023), noncompliance (GAO, 2025), inconsistencies (Ayodele et al., 2023), and information asymmetry (Arkhipova et al., 2024), resulting from inadequate onboarding and training for accounting staff. This leads to increased overall direct costs, resulting in accounting inconsistencies and noncompliance that cause financial and nonfinancial harm. The 2024 article by Tifani et al., found that a lack of training and knowledge inhibited the implementation and operation of critical corporate accounting systems.
